Meet EKX: The Internal LLM That Actually Knows SAP

Generic frontier models are great thinking partners and unreliable fact sources. There is, it turns out, a better option for SAP PMMs — and it's been hiding behind single sign-on the whole time.

By Chris O'Hara AI Lead, Data & Analytics · SAP

A few weeks ago I watched a PMM on my team — call her Maya — spend forty-five minutes trying to get ChatGPT to give her a clean list of every Joule Skill currently shipped, because she was building a one-pager for an analyst briefing and needed the numerator for a "we ship more agentic skills than [competitor]" claim. ChatGPT gave her a beautiful list of fourteen skills, six of which existed, four of which had been renamed eighteen months ago, two of which were competitor products masquerading as ours, and two of which were just made up. It was, as these things go, an entirely typical Tuesday afternoon.

The problem isn't ChatGPT. The problem is that ChatGPT has read the entire internet and doesn't particularly care which of the things it read about SAP are still true, were ever true, or are products versus marketing slides versus a Reddit thread from 2019, and for a PMM working inside an enterprise as wide and as fast-moving as SAP, the generic frontier model is a phenomenal thinking partner and a deeply unreliable fact source — which is a hard combination to manage when your job is mostly to be right about your own product.

Which is why I want to introduce you to EKX.

EKX lives at ekx.cloud.sap/chat, it sits behind SAP single sign-on (the little "Internal" badge in the header is the giveaway), and from the user's seat it looks like every other chat interface you've ever opened — a text box, a paperclip for files, a microphone, a couple of starter prompts that suggest things like "Generate a PowerPoint about S/4HANA Cloud" or "Create an interactive dashboard with all Joule Skills," and a sidebar of past conversations down the left rail. If you've used Claude or ChatGPT or Joule, you don't need a tutorial — the front door is genuinely that simple.

What's behind the front door is the interesting part.

Most chat assistants do retrieval the same boring way: they take your question, search a pile of documents, stuff the top matches into the context window, and let the LLM write something. That works fine for "what's the capital of France" and starts to fall over the moment your question requires understanding that S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition and S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition are different products, that Datasphere replaced Data Warehouse Cloud as a name change rather than a separate thing, that BDC contains both, and that Joule Skills is a class of object with members rather than a single product. EKX does retrieval differently — it's wired into SAP's internal knowledge graph, which is a structured map of every SAP product, every relationship between them, every release, every SAP Note, every integration, and when you ask it a question, EKX doesn't just grep for words; it walks the graph, figures out which entities you're actually asking about, pulls the documents associated with those entities, and only then lets the model write.

EKX answers SAP questions like someone who works at SAP, instead of like someone who once read about it.

The use cases that have changed my workflow the most are the ones where the question is shaped like "give me the actual current list of." Every Joule Skill, every BDC component, every product that integrates with a given line of business — these are exactly the questions generic LLMs are catastrophically bad at, because their failure mode is fluency, and fluency on a list question means making up plausible-sounding members. EKX can actually enumerate, because it's reading from the graph rather than free-associating from training data. The other use case I've come to rely on is battlecard fact-checking — when I need the real capability surface of an SAP product, not the marketing surface, EKX is the fastest path I've found to a defensible answer. Ask it which printing formats SAP Digital Manufacturing supports and it will hand you Adobe Forms PDF, Loftware PAS, ZPL, XSL Transformation, with SAP Note numbers attached so you can verify. Ask ChatGPT the same question and you'll get a vibes-based paragraph about how SAP supports many industry-standard formats.

It's also a surprisingly decent first-draft generator for SAP-specific decks and dashboards. Tell EKX to "generate a PowerPoint about S/4HANA Cloud" and you don't get generic positioning slop — you get grounded content pulled from the corpus that you can argue with, and the argue-with-the-draft motion is roughly forty percent of what a 10x PMM actually does all day anyway.

· · ·

A few practical notes on using it well. The @ mention in the input box lets you reference files inside the chat — drop in a competitor brief or your own draft and ask EKX to compare claims against SAP's actual capability set, which is a workflow I now run on every battlecard before it goes out. The "Balanced" toggle in the bottom right tunes how much the model leans on retrieval versus its own reasoning, and for fact-heavy questions you'll want to leave it where it is; for "help me think about positioning" questions, you'll find Claude or your assistant of choice is honestly a better thinking partner anyway, because EKX is built to retrieve, not to argue. And the Internal badge isn't decoration — outputs from EKX are grounded in internal materials, which means they're useful, accurate, and absolutely not for direct paste into customer-facing assets without going through your normal review path.

One honest caveat. EKX is still being actively tuned — the team behind it is running ongoing experiments on the best way to fuse knowledge-graph results with conventional retrieval, and you'll occasionally get an answer that's longer than it needs to be, or that buries the actual claim under three paragraphs of preamble, or that misses an entity it should have caught. It's a very good tool, not a finished one. Treat it like a sharp colleague with a great research library and an occasional tendency to over-explain — useful framing for any LLM, really, but particularly this one.

Where all of this lands for the PMM craft is in the larger pattern that the 10x PMM is the one who knows which tool to reach for. Claude for thinking, EKX for SAP truth, your own eyes for judgment, your network for taste. The PMM who's still pasting "list all SAP Joule Skills" into ChatGPT in 2026 is technically doing the same job as the PMM who got the real list out of EKX in ninety seconds — except one of them is wrong, and the other one is at lunch.

→ ekx.cloud.sap/chat Go play with it.
